title: Las Vegas insists county deal is unfair, declines to talk county's $338M claim - NewsBreak
text:
By James Schaeffer ,
1 days ago
LAS VEGAS (KLAS) -- Las Vegas City Manager Mike Janssen rejected Clark County’s claim that an attempt to amend a historic agreement over fire services is a “cash grab.” Wednesday marked the city’s turn in round three of a historically routine, public fight.
During a regularly scheduled Las Vegas City Council meeting, Janssen responded to several claims made on Tuesday by the Clark County Commission, which called the city’s amendment a “money grab.” The fight is over an interlocal agreement that manages shared land and services .
“I think it's fair to say that there's a tax being collected, $3.5 million for services that aren't being provided,” Janssen said. “If there's a ‘money grab,’ that's really the money grab.”
Download the free 8 News+ app for live newscasts and streaming originals The negotiation includes the Northwest Interlocal Fire and Rescue Services Agreement. The city’s chief complaint about the agreement is the thousands of fire calls city first responders make to the over 20,000 county residents. Simply put, city services are supporting county taxpayers.
“The city of Las Vegas is providing services to Clark County Island residents at a population that today exceeds the city of Mesquite,” Janssen said.
The City of Las Vegas proposed an amendment to the interlocal agreement which would “fix” the fire service call imbalance. Clark County is set to discuss the item once again at its commission meeting.
Both government bodies have said this debate over the interlocal agreement will not result in annexation of city or county land.
County punches back Moments after the Wednesday city meeting, Clark County released a statement saying if there were a concern about fire services to county residents, the county would act on its own.
“The County is taking swift action to create a hybrid response that places county fire trucks and contracted ambulances in proximity to these locations,” a county spokesperson wrote in a statement.
A Clark County spokesperson further wrote that the safety of county residents “will not be compromised.” The quote is a restatement from the county’s Tuesday meeting about whether fire trucks would stop at the city-county line.

The county statement ended with a reiteration that the well-being of county residents has been a paramount concern and will continue to be as discussions move forward.
City counters county’s jab Following Clark County’s reaction to the city’s meeting, Las Vegas City Hall countered the plan to move ahead without a plan.
“The City of Las Vegas wants to be clear that public safety is our top priority for all Southern Nevadans regardless of what side of an invisible line on a map that they live on,” a city spokesperson wrote in a statement.
A city spokesperson wrote that regardless of the outcome of the discussions with Clark County on the Northwest Interlocal Agreement, which the county calls the Lone Mountain Interlocal Agreement, Las Vegas Fire & Rescue will continue to respond and help residents.
“Our department is committed to responding to people regardless of where they live,” Las Vegas Fire & Rescue Chief Fernando Gray said. “One of the things I am really excited about and proud of is that not only in our region and in the valley, but our members have deployed all over the country.”
Mayor rolls with the punches Las Vegas Mayor Shelley Berkley spoke to 8 News Now about the ongoing debate over the interlocal agreement’s fire service amendment, and said the debate was simply a “family” talk gone public.
“We're two branches of the same family,” she said. “Our job is to represent our constituents.”
Berkley was asked why a fight over $3 to $5 million with the county has reached a level of public discourse. She said the issue could be characterized as something minor that becomes a debate every 10 years when the agreement is renewed by both parties.
“I believe the county is going to agree to this on the 20th,” she said. “We will have a 60-day extension where we will sit down… We want the interlocal in place. We would just like to get reimbursed for the fire service that we're providing to county residents, simple as that.”
When asked if the city was struggling financially, Berkley pointed out the city is still coming off a $286 million settlement over the Badlands Golf Course .
“Look, everybody is straining at this moment,” she said.
